content.overview: Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, of sound mind, and not disqualified from contracting by any law.

sections.heading: Minority
sections.body: A minor's agreement is void (Mohori Bibee line). Necessaries supplied may be recoverable from the minor's property (s. 68).

sections.heading: Sound mind
sections.body: Section 12: ability to understand the contract and form a rational judgment as to its effect upon the person's interests at the time of the agreement.

sections.heading: Track B
sections.body: Plead capacity; if attacking it, plead minority or unsoundness with supporting evidence. Frame necessaries and restitution carefully under ss. 68 and 64–65.

illustrations: A person who is ordinarily of unsound mind may contract during a lucid interval when capable of understanding the transaction and judging its effect; section 12 focuses on capacity at the time of contracting.

Statutory rule: Sections 11–12 determine contractual competence and soundness of mind: a person must be of majority, of sound mind and not disqualified by law; soundness is assessed by capacity to understand the contract and form a rational judgment about its effect on interests at the time of contracting.

Definition: Capacity to contract is the legal competence required to enter a binding agreement, assessed under section 11 and, for mental capacity, section 12.

Ingredients / conditions:
1. The person must have attained majority.
2. The person must be of sound mind at the time of contracting.
3. The person must not be disqualified from contracting by a law applicable to that person.
4. For section 12, the inquiry is functional: ability to understand the contract and form a rational judgment about its effect.

distinctions: Capacity to contract vs free consent: capacity concerns legal competence to contract; free consent concerns whether consent was obtained without the vitiating factors recognised by the Act.
Minority vs unsoundness of mind: both can affect capacity, but the statutory tests and consequences must be applied separately to the facts.
